rubric: PYTHON AS A FIRST LANGUAGE / BASICS / CHAPTER 1

slides.title: The first program
slides.main: A program is a list of commands the machine reads like a recipe.

items.title: print
items.sub: Prints on the screen whatever is given in parentheses

items.title: Strings
items.sub: Text lives in quotes, single or double

items.title: Comments
items.sub: Notes for people: Python doesn't read them

items.title: Arithmetic
items.sub: Calculates numbers, repeats and glues strings

body.text: Python reads almost like English: it is used for small scripts and neural networks alike. Every idea in the course is reinforced by an exercise with a real code check.

slides.title: The print command
slides.sub: Prints on the screen what it is given
slides.main: Parentheses, as in a math function: inside is what to show.

cells.title: print
cells.sub: The print command: no paper, only a screen

cells.title: Hello, world!
cells.sub: What will appear on the screen

slides.title: Strings and quotes
slides.sub: Text in quotes is called a string
slides.main: Quotes are a fence: Python treats everything inside as text, even digits.

body.text:
print("Hello!")
print('Bye!')
print("2")   # this is text, not a number

cells.sub: Single and double quotes are equal

cells.title: The same kind on both sides
cells.sub: Open and close alike, or Python gets confused

slides.title: Top-to-bottom order
slides.main: A program is a list of commands: the machine reads it like a recipe, step by step.

body.text: Runs one line at a time and prints in the same order.

slides.title: Comments
slides.sub: A hash sign hides notes for people
slides.main: A good comment explains why, not what.

body.text:
# print a hint so the user doesn't get lost
print("Enter your name")

cells.title: # comment
cells.sub: After the hash Python runs nothing

cells.title: Who they're for
cells.sub: You in a month, and a colleague today

slides.title: Print can calculate
slides.main: Parentheses change the order of operations, as in school.

body.text:
print(2 + 2)        # 4
print(2 * 3)        # 6  · multiplication is an asterisk
print((2 + 2) * 2)  # 8  · parentheses win

cells.sub: Addition and subtraction, as in school
Multiplication is an asterisk: no cross on the keyboard

slides.title: Fractional numbers
slides.main: Division always gives a fraction, even when the result is a round whole.

cells.sub: Fractions use a dot, not a comma
Whole and fractional are two kinds of numbers

slides.title: Several values
slides.main: Print puts them on one line, separated by spaces.

body.text: Value and label side by side: the screen says what it is and how much.

slides.title: Quote inside text
slides.sub: What if a quote is needed inside the string
slides.main: The fences must differ: one kind of quote outside, another inside.

slides.title: String arithmetic
slides.sub: Strings have a small arithmetic of their own
slides.main: Only plus and asterisk: strings can't be subtracted or divided.

cells.title: string * N
cells.sub: Asterisk repeats: a line of thirty dashes is one dash times thirty

cells.title: string + string
cells.sub: Plus glues two strings into one

slides.title: Empty print
slides.sub: Empty parentheses give an empty line
slides.main: Emptiness is part of the design: output, like a page, needs air.

body.text: This is how you make gaps between blocks, like paragraphs in a letter.

slides.title: Errors
slides.sub: Forget a quote or bracket and Python stops
slides.main: An error is not a failure but a pointer: read the last message, that's the point.

cells.title: Line 1
cells.sub: Python shows the line number and where it stumbled

slides.title: Summary
slides.main: The first program is ready; next it will learn to remember.

items.title: print
items.sub: Prints what it is given; commands run top to bottom

items.sub: Quotes as a fence, the same on both sides

body.text: For now every command forgets at once. Next chapter is variables: we teach the program to remember.
